hood_landmark.Old Town: Edinburgh Castle looming over the Royal Mile
hood_landmark.New Town: Georgian Princes Street with the Scott Monument's Gothic spire
hood_landmark.Leith: The Royal Yacht Britannia moored at Ocean Terminal
hood_landmark.Stockbridge: Photogenic Circus Lane and the Sunday street market
hood_landmark.Morningside: The art-deco Dominion Cinema on its village-like high street

avoid.reason: Pickpockets target Festival-season crowds on the Royal Mile and Princes Street, and Lothian Road and the Cowgate get rowdy with drinkers late at night.

hood_desc: Old Town is the historic medieval heart of the city, packed with cobbled closes, the castle and the Royal Mile; it suits first-time visitors and history lovers who want to be in the thick of the atmosphere and tourist sights.

New Town is elegant and Georgian with wide streets, upscale shopping on Princes and George Streets and refined dining; it suits travelers wanting central polish, boutique hotels and easy walking to everything.

Leith is the revitalized waterfront district with a hip, creative edge, excellent seafood, craft bars and Michelin-starred restaurants; it suits foodies and younger travelers who prefer a trendy neighborhood feel over tourist crowds.
Stockbridge is a leafy, village-like area with independent shops, delis, a Sunday market and riverside walks; it suits those seeking a relaxed, local and slightly bohemian base close to the center.

Morningside is a genteel, residential suburb with quiet tree-lined streets, cozy cafes and a comfortable local vibe; it suits longer-stay visitors and families who want calm and value away from the bustle.
lodging: Radisson Collection Hotel Royal Mile Edinburgh

water.note: Tap water is treated to strict UK standards and safe to drink.

transit.pay: Tap a contactless bank card or phone directly on buses and trams (fares auto-cap daily), or buy a Ridacard travel pass for frequent use at TravelHub kiosks. A single flat fare is about £2 (~$2.60); exact cash is also accepted on buses (no change given).
transit.hours: Trams run roughly 5am-11:30pm; Lothian's NightBus network covers the city through the early hours once daytime routes stop.

transit.m: Airlink 100 express bus to city center, 30 min
Edinburgh Trams to St Andrew Square in city center, 35 min
Lothian night bus N22 to city center, 24/7 service

food.name: Haggis, neeps and tatties
food.desc: Peppery sheep offal, oats and suet with mashed swede and potato, often with a whisky cream sauce. Far better than it sounds.

places.name: Arcade Bar Haggis and Whisky House
places.note: Off Cockburn Street; haggis several ways, including vegetarian, with a big whisky wall.

places.name: The Albanach
places.note: Whisky-focused Royal Mile bar with a well-regarded haggis plate and live music.

places.name: Howies
places.note: Scottish bistro group doing haggis as a starter and good-value set lunches.

food.name: Cullen skink
food.desc: Thick soup of smoked haddock, potato, onion and milk from the Moray coast. Smokier and heavier than chowder.

places.name: The Ship on the Shore
places.note: Seafood specialist on the Water of Leith; excellent cullen skink and oysters.

places.name: Fishers in Leith
places.note: In an old signal tower since 1991; a Leith seafood fixture.

places.name: Fishers in the City
places.note: New Town room from the Fishers seafood group; reliable cullen skink and daily fish boards.

food.name: Scottish shellfish and oysters
food.desc: West coast langoustines, Loch Fyne oysters, scallops and mussels landed a few hours away and served barely touched.

places.name: Fishers in the City
places.note: Thistle Street seafood kitchen with oysters, scallops and Scottish landings; book at weekends.

places.name: The Ship on the Shore
places.note: Champagne and seafood platters in a snug harbourside dining room.

places.name: Fishers in Leith
places.note: Reliable for scallops, mussels and daily boards from Scottish boats.

food.name: Fish supper and the deep-fried Mars bar
food.desc: Battered haddock with chips and brown sauce, and Scotland's most notorious dessert: a chocolate bar in batter, hot and molten.

places.name: Cafe Piccante
places.note: Late-night chippy best known for actually doing a proper deep-fried Mars bar.

places.name: The Clamshell
places.note: Old Town chip shop serving fish suppers and fried desserts to a post-pub crowd.

places.name: Bertie's Proper Fish and Chips
places.note: Sit-in restaurant near Victoria Street; a tidier way to eat a fish supper.

food.name: Full Scottish breakfast
food.desc: Bacon, egg, sausage, tattie scone, black pudding and often a slice of fried haggis. Built for a cold walk up Arthur's Seat.

places.name: Urban Angel
places.note: Hanover Street cafe using local, seasonal produce; long-running breakfast favourite.

places.name: Loudons
places.note: All-day brunch spot by the canal with big portions and good baking.

places.name: The Milkman
places.note: For coffee and a lighter breakfast in a tiny 1900s shopfront on the way up.

food.name: Cranachan
food.desc: Whipped cream folded with toasted oats, raspberries, honey and whisky. Scotland's traditional harvest dessert.

places.name: The Witchery by the Castle
places.note: Candlelit Gothic dining rooms by the castle esplanade; the theatrical choice.

places.name: Amber Restaurant
places.note: Inside the Scotch Whisky Experience; every dish paired with a dram.

places.name: Howies
places.note: Classic cranachan on a good-value Scottish set menu.

food.name: Single malt Scotch whisky
food.desc: Five regional styles, from light Lowland to peat-smoked Islay. Ask for a dram with a splash of water to open it up.

places.name: The Bow Bar
places.note: Small, standing-room pub with several hundred malts and no music or screens.

places.name: Whiski Rooms
places.note: Tasting flights, whisky shop and food pairings; good for a first proper dram.

places.name: Holyrood Distillery
places.note: Working distillery in a former railway building with tours and tastings.

food.name: Scottish craft ale
food.desc: Edinburgh was once a brewing capital thanks to its hard well water; cask ales and modern craft beers both thrive again.

places.name: The Hanging Bat
places.note: Lothian Road craft beer bar, run by brewer Northern Monk since 2025; long tap list and a barbecue kitchen.

places.name: Cloisters Bar
places.note: Former parsonage turned real-ale pub; nine cask lines and a big whisky shelf.

places.name: The Bow Bar
places.note: Also excellent for Scottish cask ale, poured from tall founts at the bar.

landmarks: Edinburgh Castle
A dominating fortress perched on volcanic rock overlooking the city, Scotland's most iconic historic monument.
Arthur's Seat
An extinct volcano rising above the city offering the best panoramic photo views of Edinburgh's skyline.
Royal Mile
The historic cobbled thoroughfare connecting Edinburgh Castle to Holyrood Palace, lined with medieval closes and landmarks.
Palace of Holyroodhouse
The official royal residence in Scotland, set against the backdrop of Arthur's Seat and Holyrood Park.
Calton Hill
A hill dotted with striking neoclassical monuments and the best vantage point for sunrise or sunset shots of the city.
St Giles' Cathedral
The High Kirk of Edinburgh, famed for its distinctive crown-shaped spire on the Royal Mile.
Scott Monument
A soaring Gothic Victorian spire honoring writer Sir Walter Scott, a striking landmark on Princes Street.
Princes Street Gardens
Scenic gardens beneath the Castle providing classic postcard views of the Old Town skyline.
Victoria Street
A curved, colorful row of Victorian shopfronts said to have inspired Diagon Alley, a favorite photo spot.
National Museum of Scotland
An architecturally striking museum blending Victorian and modern design in the heart of the Old Town.

dom.op: National Rail (LNER, Avanti West Coast, ScotRail, Caledonian Sleeper)

train.note: No trains run directly abroad from Edinburgh - for the Eurostar to Paris, Brussels or Amsterdam you change at London St Pancras. LNER reaches London King's Cross in about 4h20 from Edinburgh Waverley, and the Caledonian Sleeper overnight train runs Edinburgh to London Euston nightly except Saturdays (https://www.sleeper.scot/).

bus.note: There are no direct international coaches from Edinburgh; for Europe you connect in London. Long-distance domestic coaches to London and English cities are run by National Express (https://www.nationalexpress.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.co.uk/) and Megabus (https://uk.megabus.com/), from the Edinburgh Bus Station at St Andrew Square.

ferry.note: Edinburgh has no direct international passenger ferry. The old Rosyth-Zeebrugge passenger link (near Edinburgh) ended years ago, and a proposed DFDS Rosyth-Dunkirk service has repeatedly slipped and is not confirmed as running in 2026. The nearest routes to mainland Europe currently sail from English ports such as Newcastle (DFDS to Amsterdam).

half.name: Stirling Castle
half.blurb: This mighty hilltop fortress guarded Scotland's heart and hosted kings amid sweeping views over historic battlefields.

half.name: St Andrews
half.blurb: Golf's birthplace pairs cathedral ruins, a clifftop castle and honey-stone lanes beside wide North Sea beaches.

half.name: Loch Lomond
half.blurb: Scotland's largest loch shimmers below wooded hills, dotted with islands and framed by Highland scenery.

half.name: North Berwick
half.blurb: A breezy seaside town with sandy beaches, seabird colonies and views to volcanic Bass Rock.

half.name: Glasgow
half.blurb: Scotland's largest city buzzes with Victorian architecture, lively music venues and grand riverside streets.

half.name: The Kelpies
half.blurb: Two towering steel horse heads rise beside a canal, alongside the ingenious rotating Falkirk Wheel.
